title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page of E506. The modern reading of each step follows.

**The problem.** Integrate the separated equation dx/√X = dy/√Y, where X and Y are the same quartic, in x and in y respectively:
X = A + Bx + Cx² + Dx³ + Ex⁴ and Y = A + By + Cy² + Dy³ + Ey⁴.
This is Euler's own problem from the 1750s: the addition theorem for elliptic integrals of the first kind.

**Euler's admission.** He says that he had laboured long over this equation. In particular he had sought, in vain, a *direct* method that would lead to its integral by an easy and plain road. He says he was astonished to learn that Lagrange had found such a method in volume IV of the Miscellanea Taurinensia.

**Lagrange's result as quoted.** The complete algebraic integral is
(√X + √Y)/(x − y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²),
where Δ is the arbitrary constant. Equivalently, ((√X+√Y)/(x−y))² − D(x+y) − E(x+y)² is a first integral.

**Background to Lagrange's method.** Lagrange introduces an auxiliary variable t with dx/dt = √X and dy/dt = √Y, so that d²x/dt² = X′/2. He then passes to p = x + y and q = x − y. From this he obtains a second-order relation that admits an integrating combination. Euler (§2, next page) classifies this as a 'third way' of integrating: neither separation of variables nor an integrating factor, but differentiation. In §4 he begins to verify the integral by squaring and differentiating so as to eliminate Δ.

**Check of correctness.** Take A = 1, C = −1, all other coefficients 0, and set x = sin α, y = sin β. Then
(cos α + cos β)/(sin α − sin β) = cot((α − β)/2),
which is constant exactly when α − β is constant. That is the solution of dx/√(1−x²) = dy/√(1−y²). So the sign convention (√X + √Y with x − y, for the equation with an equals sign rather than a sum equal to zero) is consistent.

**General check by degree.** V²/(x−y)² − D(x+y) − E(x+y)² is a known first integral (Lagrange 1766–69). The coefficients A, B and C do not appear explicitly in it, as stated.
errors: The title prints (or the scan shows) 'du/√Y' where the text means dy/√Y. This is a typographical slip in the title; §1 correctly has dy/√Y.
No mathematical errors on this page. The quoted Lagrange integral is correct for dx/√X = dy/√Y.

ideas.what: The differential equation dx/√X = dy/√Y with X and Y the same quartic, which has an algebraic complete integral
ideas.modern_name: Euler's addition theorem for elliptic integrals of the first kind
ideas.where_published: E251, E252, E261, E264 and the Institutiones calculi integralis, vol. I

ideas.what: Lagrange's integral (√X+√Y)/(x−y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²), obtained by a 'direct' method using an auxiliary variable
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's direct/mechanical proof of the elliptic addition theorem
ideas.where_published: E506 itself; Euler also discusses it in related later papers on the same topic

ideas.what: Classification of integration methods into separation of variables, integrating factor, and integration by differentiation
ideas.modern_name: Methods of solving ODEs (differentiation method / first integrals)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the introductory page restating Lagrange's well-known integral and Euler's reaction to it. Both are thoroughly documented in the histories of elliptic functions, so nothing here is new.
transcription_corrections: Title: 'du/√Y' should read dy/√Y (a slip in the print or the scan); the transcription faithfully reproduces 'du'.
Line-order garbling in the scan of §1: 'penitus obstupui', 'Miscellaneorum Taurinensium' and 'algebraicum' are split across lines. The transcription reconstructs these correctly.
